response: Good effort working night by night, Luca—just remember to include the original vampires, and remember that all 12 vampires can turn people on the second night. After night 1, there are \(2+2\times5=12\) vampires; after night 2, there are \(12+12\times5=\boxed{72}\) vampires.

Good effort, but your equation simplifies to \(110=110\), so it doesn’t determine \(x\); also, \((110-2\cdot55)/3=0\), not 20. If \(x\) is the number of rounds they work **together**, use \(2x+3x=110\), so \(5x=110\) and \(\boxed{x=22}\)—it will take **22 rounds**.

You’re very close, Steven—you correctly found 1,600 gallons for today and 2,400 gallons for tomorrow’s 600 miles. Since the question asks for the total over **both days**, add them: \(1{,}600 + 2{,}400 = \boxed{4{,}000\text{ gallons}}\).

Great work adding the totals, Jordy: there are 46 males and 48 females. The 46 males can pair with 46 females, leaving \(48-46=2\) females without partners, so only **2 students** are unable to pair—you counted the same two extra females twice.

Great work on the first two steps, Seth—Cyrus got 24 bites, so his family got 12 altogether. Since those 12 bites were shared only among the **6 other people**, not Cyrus, calculate \(12 \div 6 = 2\), so each family member got **2 mosquito bites**.

You made a good start by finding that Winston used \(6+2=8\) gallons, but that means he has \(10-8=2\) gallons left, so 4 gallons isn’t correct. To fill the 12-gallon tank, he needs \(12-2=\boxed{10}\) gallons; your earlier \(12-10=2\) only compared the tank’s capacity with the gas he started with.

Great job, Riya—your reasoning and calculations are correct! The company produced \(3 \times 7{,}000 = 21{,}000\) rolls per day, so March’s total was \(21{,}000 \times 31 = \boxed{651{,}000}\) toilet paper rolls.

Great job adding the pages read so far to get 262! Since the average is over all **7 days** of the week—including Wednesday, when he read 0—Berry’s goal is \(7 \times 50 = 350\) pages, so he needs to read \(350 - 262 = \boxed{88}\) pages on Saturday.

You’ve shown your algebra clearly, Scott, but the setup doesn’t match the givens: the right-hand angle is \(60^\circ\), so the left angle is \(2(60^\circ)=120^\circ\), and the stated total would give a top angle of \(250^\circ-120^\circ-60^\circ=70^\circ\). Do check the problem’s wording, though, because an actual triangle’s angles sum to \(180^\circ\); with these givens, that would leave \(0^\circ\) for the top, so the problem as written does not describe a valid triangle.
Great job finding that Tanya has 10 red erasers! Remember that Rachel has three less than **half** of those 10, so Rachel has \(10 \div 2 - 3 = 2\), and Hanna has \(2 \times 2 = \boxed{4}\) erasers.
You’re right to use the 52 weeks in a year, Brenda, but the club has \(3\times2+5+2=13\) members, not 10. Ron gets a turn every 13 weeks, so he picks a book \(52\div13=\boxed{4}\) times a year.

You’re off to a great start—16 scallops is correct, but the $6 you calculated is the cost of **2 scallops**, not 1 scallop. Nate needs 8 two-scallop servings, so the total cost is \(8 \times \$6 = \boxed{\$48}\).

Good effort setting up an equation, Heidi, but remember that the 4 hours is only the trip to lunch, so the full trip there and back takes \(4\times2=8\) hours. Since that round trip is half his reading time, the book takes \(16\) hours to read, meaning Juan reads \(4000\div16=\boxed{250}\) pages per hour.

You’ve made a good start, but Friday should be compared with Wednesday alone: \(2+3=5\) hours, and each day should be counted only once. The total is \(2+2+5=9\) hours, so the average is \(9\div3=\boxed{3\text{ hours per day}}\).

Your arithmetic is correct, DeAndre, but this is an **inverse** relationship: with more pugs working, the cleaning should take less time, not more. The job requires \(4 \times 45 = 180\) pug-minutes, so 15 pugs need \(180 \div 15 = \boxed{12\text{ minutes}}\).

Your first two steps were correct: 60% of students remain, and splitting them into two equal groups gives 30% in each group. Since only one group attends on a given day, you can stop there—**30% of students are present in school**, so the final division by 2 was unnecessary.
Great work finding that 36 balloons touch the ceiling and 14 do not. To find how many more, subtract the two groups: \(36-14=22\), so there are **22 more balloons** touching the ceiling.

You correctly found that his brother’s score would rise to 15, so Levi needs a total of at least \(15 + 5 = 20\) baskets to be 5 ahead. Since Levi has already scored 8, he must score \(20 - 8 = \boxed{12}\) more times.

Nice start, Rishi—you’re right that Jake needs 20 washes, but $4.00 is the cost per **bottle**, not per wash. Since \(20 \div 4 = 5\), he needs 5 bottles and spends \(5 \times \$4.00 = \boxed{\$20.00}\).

Great work finding the 25 texts and the 3 police texts—just remember that your subtotal of 30 already includes the first 5 and the 25, so adding 25 again counts them twice. The total is \(30+3=\boxed{33}\) texts.

Your month-by-month reasoning is great—the only slip is using \(3 \times 30\) for months 2–3, which is just **two** months. So the total is \(10 + (2 \times 30) + 45 + (2 \times 30) = \boxed{\$175}\).

You’re on the right track: the weekdays total 10 hours, and multiplying the weekly total by 4 is the correct final step. Just check the weekend addition—10 + 3 = 13 hours per week, so Percy swims 13 × 4 = **52 hours** over 4 weeks.

You’re on the right track, but don’t forget the 3 cookies Lou ate on the first day: he ate \(3+1=4\) cookies altogether, and the 2 he returned were no longer missing. So \(4+7=11\) cookies were missing; since that was half the jar, the jar originally held 22 cookies, and **11 cookies remained**.

You’ve tracked the first two hours correctly, but the tank keeps losing 2 gallons during hours three and four as well. Including that leak, hour three ends with \(36-2+1=35\) gallons, and hour four ends with \(35-2+3=\boxed{36}\) gallons.

You’re off to a good start, but \(13{,}200 \div 2 = 6{,}600\) is the total tilling distance in feet, not the number of swaths. Since each foot takes 2 seconds, the total time is \(6{,}600 \times 2 = 13{,}200\) seconds, which is \(\boxed{220\text{ minutes}}\).

You’re on the right track, but Ignatius’s 4 bicycles have \(4\times2=8\) tires, so his friend’s cycles have \(3\times8=24\) tires. Subtracting the unicycle and tricycle tires leaves \(24-1-3=20\) tires for bicycles, so the friend owns \(20\div2=\boxed{10}\) bicycles.

Great work finding Sammy’s score of 28 points, Ayisha! Since the exam was worth 35 points, Sammy lost \(35-28=7\) points, so he made **7 mistakes**—you can subtract directly without using \(7-x\) or an inequality.

Nice work finding that Sangita has 1,320 hours left, but dividing by 24 weeks gives hours per **week**, not hours per month. Since she has 6 months, calculate \(1{,}320 \div 6 = 220\), so she must fly **220 hours per month**.
Great reasoning, Stephanie—your method is correct, and there’s just one small slip in the final subtraction. Since \(125 - 100 = 25\), the five bottles will be **$25 more expensive** in two months.

You’re right that each glass contains 8 ounces, but the milk and syrup can’t simply be pooled because every glass must use them in a fixed ratio. The milk makes \(130 \div 6.5 = 20\) glasses, while the syrup could make \(60 \div 1.5 = 40\), so the milk runs out first and Charles drinks \(20 \times 8 = \boxed{160}\) ounces of chocolate milk, with 30 ounces of syrup left over.

You’ve set up the multiplication nicely, but remember that Wanda walks **to school and back home** both in the morning and afternoon, so she walks \(0.5+0.5=1\) mile each trip, or \(2\) miles per day. Therefore, she walks \(2\times5\times4=\boxed{40\text{ miles}}\) after 4 weeks.

Your dinner calculations are correct, DeAndre, but breakfast and lunch need to be counted for **all seven days**, not just once. Try calculating \(7\times20\) for breakfast and \(7\times5\) for lunch, then add your dinner total of \(40+90=130\) minutes—what total do you get?

Nice work finding the $0.56 change, but your coins total only $0.31, and after your last step you still have $0.25 left to return. Use two quarters for $0.50, then one nickel and one penny for the remaining $0.06, so Rosie gets **4 coins**—the smallest number possible.

Nice work finding Jake’s total time: \(270 \div 3 = 90\) seconds; since Austin takes 60 seconds, Jake arrives \(90-60=\boxed{30}\) seconds later. You don’t need Austin’s “steps per second” rate, because he travels by elevator rather than on the stairs.

Your coin calculations are correct, but **each** piggy bank holds both 100 pennies and 50 dimes, so each contains $1 + $5 = $6. Since Ivan fills **two** piggy banks, he has \(2 \times \$6 = \boxed{\$12}\).

Nice start, Alejandra—subtracting 17 was correct, but \(26+22-17=31\) already includes the people who took both drinks, so adding 17 again counts them twice. As a check, there were \(26-17=9\) wine-only and \(22-17=5\) soda-only people, giving \(9+5+17=\boxed{31}\) people altogether.

Great start, but remember that the 4 hours is only for the trip to get lunch, so going there and back takes \(4 \times 2 = 8\) hours. Since that is half his reading time, he reads for 16 hours, so he reads \(4000 \div 16 = \boxed{250}\) pages per hour.

You’re on the right track by finding that Mike kept 4 rose bushes, but your $650 total includes all 6 bushes, including the 2 for his friend. For himself, he spent \(4 \times \$75 + 2 \times \$100 = \$300 + \$200 = \boxed{\$500}\).

You’re on the right track by splitting the children into groups of 6 and 2, but each of those 6 children has 8 children—there’s no need to subtract 1. Therefore, Max has \(6\times8+2\times5=48+10=\boxed{58}\) grandchildren.

Nice start, Seth—\(672 \div 4 = 168\) already gives the number of balloons of each color, so there are 168 yellow balloons and you don’t need to divide by 4 again. Anya took home half of them: \(\frac{1}{2}\times168=\boxed{84}\) balloons.

Nice work on the first cut—she donates 50 square inches and keeps 50 square inches. The second time, she cuts the **50 square inches she kept**, so she donates \(50 \div 2 = 25\) more square inches, for a total of \(50 + 25 = \boxed{75}\) square inches donated.

Great start finding the 30 oz maximum, Mariana, but remember that the 10 oz on the pancakes also counts toward what Don has consumed. After eating them, he will have had \(12 + 10 = 22\) oz, so he can have \(30 - 22 = \boxed{8\text{ oz}}\) more.

Great start finding the $10.50 wood cost per birdhouse; since profit is added to the cost, the selling price is $10.50 + $5.50 = $16.00, not $5.00. Therefore, Denver will charge Danny $16.00 × 2 = **$32.00** for two birdhouses.

You’ve set up the steps well, Rishi, but there’s a small multiplication error: \(0.2 \times 5 = 1\) kg per meal, not 2 kg. The bag therefore lasts \(42 \div 1 = 42\) household meals, and \(42 \div 14 = \boxed{3\text{ weeks}}\).
You made a good start by finding \(6\times6=36\), but 36 is the number being doubled, not the total after adding 20. Instead, calculate \(2(36)+20=92\), so Wendy needs to carry **92 books**.

Great reasoning so far, Brenda—your $1 profit per candle is correct! Since 20 candles require 2 pounds of beeswax, supplies cost 2 × $10 = $20, so Charlie’s net profit is $40 − $20 = **$20**, which also matches 20 × $1.
You’re on the right track with your setup, but your answer doesn’t check: \(4+5-3=6\), not 12. Use \(x+5-3=12\), which simplifies to \(x+2=12\), so \(x=10\); Julia’s package contained **10 spoons**.

Seth, you’re carefully tracking all the notes, but the 220 she used must be subtracted from her total supply, giving the equation \(80+x-220=23\). Solving, \(x=23+220-80=163\), so the package contained **163 Post-it notes**.

You’re very close, Michael—your weekday calculation is correct, but the soda replaces his dinner water, so it shouldn’t be counted as water. John drinks 3 glasses of water on each weekend day, giving \(20 + 2 \times 3 = \boxed{26}\) glasses of water for the week.

Your strategy is clear, Mariana—just check the units: each household meal uses \(5\times0.2=1\) kg, so the \(2\) kg you found is the amount eaten in one day (lunch and dinner). Therefore, the bag lasts \(42\div2=21\) days, and \(21\div7=\boxed{3\text{ weeks}}\).

You’re off to a good start by finding 24 pencils in Jam’s boxes; since those pencils fill 3 boxes, each box holds \(24 \div 3 = 8\) pencils. Including the 2 loose pencils, Jam and Meg have \(26 + 46 = 72\) pencils altogether, so they need \(72 \div 8 = \boxed{9}\) boxes.

You correctly found the $120,000 increase and Josh’s $130,000 total cost, but the house’s new value is its original $80,000 value plus that increase—not the increase plus his costs. The repaired house is worth $200,000, so his profit is $200,000 − $130,000 = **$70,000**.

You’re on the right track with the $50 increases, Ayisha, but you counted only the three other people’s bids; Carmen also bids after each of them, making six increases after her opening $200 bid. Try listing all seven bids in order—what do you get for Carmen’s final winning bid?

Great start—you correctly found that Brian has \(20-5=15\) games after the loss, so use 15, not 20, since that is his amount when the comparison is made. Therefore, Bobby has \(3(15)-5=45-5=\boxed{40}\) video games.

You chose the right formulas—just convert the length to feet **before** dividing, since 3 yards = 9 feet. The width is \(360 \div 9 = 40\) feet, so the perimeter is \(2(9+40)=\boxed{98\text{ feet}}\).

Great work finding that Elliott had taken 6,000 steps before his jog; the 4,000 steps remaining at that point include both his jog and the 2,000 steps still left afterward. Therefore, he took \(4{,}000-2{,}000=\boxed{2{,}000}\) steps during his jog.

You’ve calculated the floor counts and the last two travel times correctly—nice work! The first 10 floors take 15 minutes **in total**, not 15 minutes per floor, so the total time is \(15+25+80=120\) minutes, or \(120\div60=\boxed{2\text{ hours}}\).

Nice start finding Monday’s 18-situp shortfall, Jordy, but the goal is 30 situps **each day**, so Tuesday also leaves a shortfall of \(30-19=11\); her two-day total shouldn’t be compared with just one day’s goal. To meet Wednesday’s goal and make up both shortfalls, Shawna must do \(30+18+11=\boxed{59}\) situps.

Nice start—your $900 snack total is correct, but remember that each of the six members also pays for six hardcover and six paperback books. Each member pays \(150+6(30)+6(12)=402\) dollars, so Niles collects \(6\times402=\boxed{\$2{,}412}\) in total.

Great work calculating the contributions and finding that Lisa had $3,360 in total. Since she was still **$400 short**, the gift must cost $400 **more** than that amount, so add instead of subtract: **$3,360 + $400 = $3,760**.
Great job setting up the problem, DeAndre—your three amounts are correct! Check the final addition: $8 + $6 + $18 = $32, so Mrs. Martin pays the cashier **$32**.

Great reasoning, Luca—your steps are correct: \(50+30=80\), and doubling that gives \(160\) racers. You just made a subtraction error at the end: \(160-130=30\), so **30 people** dropped out before finishing the race.

Nice work identifying that Jenny had \(\frac47\) of her money left; since that remaining amount is $24, the equation should be \(\frac47x=24\) (while \(x-24\) represents the \(\frac37\) she spent). Solving gives \(x=42\), so half of her original amount is **$21**.

Great job setting up the variables and remembering to include the dogs, Lakisha! Since the cats and two dogs make six four-legged pets, use \(x+2=6\), so \(x=4\); Frankie therefore has 4 cats, 10 snakes, 3 parrots, and 2 dogs, for a total of \(\boxed{19}\) pets.

Great strategy, Heidi, but rounding the decimals and mixing hours with minutes caused an error; instead, the activities total \(120+240+30+40+70=500\) minutes, while the flight lasts \(680\) minutes. That leaves \(680-500=180\) minutes, so Aren has exactly **3 hours** to nap.

Great start finding 100 students altogether; since those students are shared among 4 classrooms, you should divide by 4 rather than assume 50 boys and 50 girls or multiply by 4. Therefore, \(100 \div 4 = 25\), so there are **25 students in each classroom**.
Great job calculating all three weights correctly! The lightest pumpkin is actually Jessica’s at 27 pounds, so the difference is \(108 - 27 = \boxed{81}\) pounds.
Excellent, Scott! That means Nigel has \(90+10=100\) dollars now, so if \(x\) is the amount he gave away, can you solve \(45-x+80=100\) to find \(x\)?
Great work, DeAndre! He spent $10,000 + $20,000 = $30,000 and recovered $5,000, so he is out of pocket $30,000 − $5,000 = **$25,000**.

I see your thinking, but since Gavin had twice as many dreams last year as this year, multiplying 1,460 by 2 gives last year’s 2,920 dreams—not the two-year total. Now add this year’s dreams: 1,460 + 2,920 = **4,380 dreams** in all.
That’s right, Luca! Since each barrel takes 3 minutes on a normal day, how long would it take to fill all 12 barrels?

Good job checking your work, but \(3\times60\) isn’t the right correction: Martha’s hold time was \(6\times10=60\) minutes. She then spent \(60\div2=30\) minutes yelling, so the total was \(10+60+30=\boxed{100\text{ minutes}}\).
That’s right—Billy needs to make up those 12 minutes by washing dishes. Since each dish takes 2 minutes, how many dishes should he wash?
Great thinking—doubling both kinds of paintings works here and will also double his total sales. Now calculate \(16 \times \$60 + 8 \times \$30\); what do you get for this month’s sales?

Thank you for explaining—your reasoning is correct, and I’m sorry for suggesting otherwise. The green turtles are 1 part (800), the hawksbills are 2 parts (1,600), and together they make 3 parts: \(800+1{,}600=\boxed{2{,}400}\) turtles.

You’re on the right track, but your sequence shows only three “hushes”; six hushes means the terrier barked \(2 \times 6 = 12\) times. Since the poodle barked twice for each terrier bark, the poodle barked \(2 \times 12 = \boxed{24}\) times.
Great job, Heidi! The total cost is $100 + $50 = $150, so how much does James pay when that amount is split evenly between two people?

You correctly found that Barney uses 14 towels in a week, but the other 4 towels are still **clean**; the 14 used towels are dirty. After missing laundry, those 4 clean towels last \(4 \div 2 = 2\) days, so he will have no clean towels for the remaining \(7-2=\boxed{5}\) days.
You’re very close, Cody—just remember to subtract the 3 spoons Julia used before counting the 12 she had left. The equation is \(x+5-3=12\), so \(x=10\); Julia’s package contained **10 spoons**.

You’ve correctly counted 20 glasses on weekdays, but remember there are **two** weekend days. He drinks 3 glasses of water on both Saturday and Sunday, so the total is \(20 + 2(3) = \boxed{26}\) glasses of water.

Good effort, DeAndre—after four weeks Josh has \(3+4=7\) balls, and dropping 3 leaves \(7-3=4\) balls for him to juggle. The two caught by the crowd and the one lost are not returned to him on stage, so the answer is **4 balls**.
You’re using the right relationship, but the comparison uses Brian’s total **after** he lost 5 games: \(20-5=15\). So Bobby has \(3(15)-5=\boxed{40}\) video games.

Your setup is exactly right: \(240 \times 50 = 12{,}000\) gummy bears, and dividing by \(300\) gummy bears per minute gives the time. Just recheck the final division: \(12{,}000 \div 300 = 40\), so the factory would take **40 minutes**, not 0.67 minutes.

Great job, Seth—your multiplication method works perfectly! After the increase, the company made \(7{,}000 \times 3 = 21{,}000\) rolls per day, so its total for March was \(21{,}000 \times 31 = \boxed{651{,}000}\) rolls.
That’s exactly right, Luca—well done for correcting your calculation! There are **37 students in class C**, and the check \(32 + 11 + 37 = 80\) confirms your answer.

Good thinking to use doubling, Claire, but \(50 \times 2^4 = 800\), not 480. Instead, work backward by halving: \(480 \to 240 \to 120 \to 60 \to 30\), so the count first drops below 50 **4 days ago**, when there were 30 zombies.
You’re on the right track—subtracting 26 from both sides gives \(2x = 20\), not \(x = 20\). Now divide both sides by 2 to get \(x = 10\), so **10 customers** bought two watermelons.
I’m glad algebra helped you organize your thinking, Hunter. Since \(4\times7=28\) people wear horizontal stripes, \(40-7-28=5\), so **5 people wear vertical stripes**—nice step-by-step reasoning!
Great! Please walk me through the steps on your whiteboard and share your final answer so we can check your reasoning together.
Good try! You calculated \(5+4=9\), but \(5\times4\) means \(5+5+5+5\), which equals **20**.
Good try—9 is \(3^2\), since \(3\times3=9\). For \(3^3\), multiply three factors of 3: \(3\times3\times3=27\), so \(3^3=27\).
Before you finalize your answer, recheck by counting the sides carefully—remember, an octagon has 8 sides. Tell me what you count, and we’ll make sure your reasoning supports your answer.
Yes, picture 3 is correct—the square has more than one line of symmetry. In fact, it has four: two diagonals and two lines through the midpoints of opposite sides.
Great—your final answer is confirmed, and you’ve earned 2 points. Nice work!
Good job, plus one point! To help us identify the shape, are all four angles right angles?

All right—thank you for giving it your best effort today! We’ll review the solution together next session; for now, remember to re-read the question, check each calculation, and confirm that your answer has the correct units.
